chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father and a number of our companions, all from Al-Hasan ibn Mahboub, from Ali ibn Ra'ab, from Abu Hamza, from Ali ibn Al-Husayn (peace be upon him), who said:

Amir Al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) used to say: 'Time is but three days. The past day has gone with what was in it and will not return. If you did good in it, you will not grieve its departure but rejoice in what it brought; if you were negligent in it, your regret for its departure will be severe due to your negligence.'

And you are in your day, which you have entered from tomorrow, in a state of surprise, not knowing if you will reach it. And if you do reach it, perhaps your share of negligence in it will be like your share of negligence in the past day.

So one of the three days has passed, in which you were negligent; and a day you await, in which you are not certain of leaving negligence. And it is your day which you have entered. It is fitting for you to use your intellect and reflect on what you neglected in the past day: the good deeds you failed to acquire and the evil deeds you failed to avoid.

And with this, while facing tomorrow, you are without confidence in reaching it and without certainty of acquiring a good deed or turning away from a frustrating evil. Thus, you are in your day which you face as in your day which you left behind. So act like a man who hopes from the days only for the day he wakes in and its night. So act or leave it, and Allah is the Helper in that.

key_terms.الْمُؤْتَمِنُ: The one who trusts (contextual: confidence in reaching tomorrow)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic perspective on the three days of time according to Imam Ali?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi emphasizes the concept of 'ghurrah' (deception) of the present day, urging believers to treat the current day as their final opportunity for accountability. It highlights the Shia scholarly focus on balancing reflection on past deeds with the uncertainty of the future, advocating for a state of constant readiness (yaqazah) in the present. The narration serves as a practical guide for spiritual self-assessment, linking daily actions to eternal consequences.
